newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian govt aims for native title clarity.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian govt aims for native title clarity.

text.p: The Australian Federal government aims to clarify uncertainty over native land title, which it will discuss with states at a Sydney meeting on Wednesday.

Asked what he expected from the meeting, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer told Reuters: "Hopefully a commonsense outcome and one which will meet the objectives of providing clarity, certainty, consistency and a clear-cut control arrangement which is not unreasonable for Aboriginals and non-Aboriginals."

In December the High Court, Australia's supreme tribunal, ruled that traditional Aboriginal ownership of land, which it had invented in 1992, existed even when a state government had leased the land to pastoralists.

After the 1992 decision -- the Mabo case, in which the court said Aborigines might still own their traditional lands if they had kept up a continuing association with it -- it was assumed that a pastoral lease terminated native title.
If it had, then pastoralists and mining companies using former pastoral land would have the exclusive use of the land they had always assumed they had.

But in December -- in the Wik case, named after the Wik aboriginal people, who were litigants -- the court ruled that leases and the native title existed together, giving aborigines some kind of right to access and, when the leases expired, full ownership.
The exact rights of the Aborigines are unclear, and primary producers and some states say the resulting uncertainty is enough to discourage investment.
So the meeting is supposed to settle the situation.
In theory, the Federal and state parliaments could simply abolish native title, but that would amount to bluntly depriving Aborigines, already a highly disadvantaged group, of their property.

An alternative, backed by some states, is to codify the Aborigines' rights in legislation, producing a system similar to what is already operating in Western Australia, where Aborigines have traditional access to pastoral and mining land.
But Queensland, with major primary industries, does not have such a system.
If the parliaments take away any rights, they will have to pay for them, as they did in 1993 when they negotiated away some of the entitlements established in the Mabo case.
Before the Mabo case it was assumed that the Crown owned all land upon Australia's European settlement in 1788, and for more than 200 years it was bought and sold accordingly.
The 1993 settlement involved marathon parliamentary sittings.
The former Labor government had to bring together the conflicting demands of the Aborigines, primary producers and the states that generally backed them.
Some Aboriginal entitlements were withdrawn, a compensation fund created and a regular process instituted for pursuing claims.
